title: The Crank, Then the Cans
passages:
Dray never touched the plate. He stood on his running board forty meters out, hands folded on the rail, while the lamp on the dirt threw his shadow long across the ore. "That's a jaw crank," he said. "Socket drive, three flats. Turns the clamp pin a quarter at a time so a loader doesn't get a hand taken off."

"It's a door crank," Brill said, "and the door's mine."

"It's a crank." He said it the way he'd read a number off a page.

Brill did the sum she always did, and hated. Two names on her board: Miko Keres in ink, herself in her own hand. Saul at her shoulder with a look that said *don't*, because Saul had been raised on that look working. Call a name out on the steel and the man on the running board wrote it down and drove off with it, and she'd have a storeroom full of cans and no one to open them.

"Saul," she said. "Shop. Bring the come-along." The come-along was a hand winch, a chain hoist with a ratchet you pumped by arm, and it hung on a nail where it had hung since the pump died.

Then she went down on her knees at the clamp with the crank and backed the pin off four flats, slow, the way you do when the thing you're loosening is holding eleven cans and one of them is wrong. The spoiled can sat against the pin, sweating, a fat bead running its seam. The clamp came slack. The jaw did not open. It stayed shut, pin in its hole, no matched seal, no receiving mark, nothing handed over.

She stood, and put her boot against the crank, and slid it down the ore dirt.

"You're giving me a tool," Dray said.

"I'm not holding anything tight," Brill said. "That's all. What you do with slack is your business."

He came off the running board, which was as far as he came, crouched, picked the crank up in his right hand, and put it inside his coat. He did not cross the plate. He walked back to the board and stood on it again.

Saul came out with the come-along and stopped, reading the slack clamp, reading her face.

"Ten good cans," Brill said. "Roll two to his board by hand. Not one more."

"Two," Dray agreed. "I'll strap them myself."

Miko laughed, one short note. "You're paying a man to take your cans."

"I'm paying him to keep standing where he is."

The spoiled can shifted on the slack clamp with a sound like a wet rope. Everyone heard it. A needle on the jaw's little brass gauge, the one nobody had read in a year because nobody had needed to, went up a hair.

"That one's going," Miko said.

"That one's mine too," Dray said.

Brill turned on her. "Don't help."

"Wasn't going to." Miko tipped her chin at the plate. "Forty minutes, maybe less, before the seam lets go, and then your jaw's got a hole in it and he's got a lamp and three weeks of fuel." She shrugged. "I'm just saying the math out loud. You people like the math."

Dray set the lamp a little straighter on the dirt.

"Draw your cans, loader," he said. "I'm counting."

Saul hooked the come-along’s chain to the lower lug of the jaw and pumped the ratchet by arm. The chain groaned against the steel. The pin shifted, then the clamp went slack enough that Miko could slide her fingers under the nearest canister. It was scuffed, still warm from the line, its seam holding. She put her shoulder to it and rolled it out onto the ore dirt. The rim made a low hum against the ground. Saul took the second can while she kept the come-along from jumping its track. Between them they walked both cans to Dray’s running board, one on each side of the lamp’s pool of light.

The spoiled can stayed on the clamp, sweating against the pin. A fat dark bead ran its seam and broke onto the jaw’s little brass gauge, the one nobody had read in a year because nobody had needed to. Miko watched the needle tremble but not move.

Dray did not step off the board. He held a length of black webbing, the kind riggers use to lash cargo so it won’t shift in a turn.

“Two,” he said. “Counted.”

“We counted,” Miko said, wiping her palms on her coveralls. “You wanted two good cans. You got them.”

He knelt, looped the strap over the first can, pulled it through the buckle, and cinched it tight against the rail. He did the same with the second, checking each buckle twice. He stood, brushed his hands on his coat, and folded his arms.

“A trade taken isn’t a bargain kept,” Dray said.

Brill’s mouth tightened. “You took the cans.”

“I took what I came for,” Dray said. “My bargain was struck for a name. You never said one.”

“You said a trade,” Brill said.

“I said my terms,” Dray said. “You didn’t meet them.”

Miko looked from the strapped cans to the spoiled one still dripping on the pin. “You’re going to let it rot in the jaw rather than open it for two good cans?”

“I’m going to wait,” Dray said. “I have fuel and no schedule.”

The spoiled can let go another drip onto the clamp pin. It hissed once, soft.

Dray tapped the coat pocket where he’d put the crank. “Your jaw stays shut until someone says a name on the steel. That’s the yard’s rule. That’s my rule.”

He didn’t cross the plate. He didn’t look at the rig behind him. He stood on the running board and waited, hands folded on the rail, while the lamp on the dirt threw his shadow long across the ore.

Miko reached for the snap at her collar and worked the badge free. C9-047, stamped in aluminum, still warm from her body heat, the corners scratched where it had rubbed against her coveralls. She held it out toward Dray’s running board.

“Take it,” she said. “My name, my number, my station. Open the jaw.”

Dray didn’t move. His hands stayed folded on the rail.

Brill crossed the ore dirt in three steps. She clamped her work glove over Miko’s mouth before Miko could say another word, hard enough to tilt her head back. The glove smelled of grease and starch.

“That badge was bought with three coast tickets I burned in my own stove,” Brill said, her voice low against Miko’s ear. “I paid for it. It’s mine, not yours. You don’t get to spend what you didn’t earn.”

Miko twisted against the glove, eyes wide. She tapped once against Brill’s wrist: *let go*.

Brill didn’t. “You want a name on a plate? You got your name written in ink on my storeroom board because I let you. That ink can wash out same as pencil.”

Saul spoke from the come-along chain, not looking up from the ratchet. “A name in pencil won’t hold a wire,” he said. “Dray’s book is ink or nothing, and you’re not ink yet.”

Brill eased the glove off but kept a hand on Miko’s shoulder, steering her back toward the door plate. “You walk off my station with my badge in your hand and Dray writes you down as salvage. We’re not doing that.”

Miko spat dirt from her lip. “You’re letting him sit there with two of my cans and a rotten third while you protect a piece of metal.”

“I’m letting him wait,” Brill said. “He’s got fuel and no schedule. We’ve got a jaw and a spoiled can. The math was always going to be ugly. Now it’s uglier.”

Dray tapped the pocket where the crank rested. “Still waiting on a name,” he said.

Miko looked from Brill’s fingers to the strapped cans on Dray’s rail. The spoiled can let go another drip onto the clamp pin. It hissed against the brass gauge. The needle jumped once, then settled.

Behind them, down the ore grade, something shifted in the dark beyond the lamp’s pool. Miko turned her head, but Brill’s hand pressed her back toward the plate.

“Not yet,” Brill said. “Dray, you want a name? Here’s one: Miko Keres, station loader, badge C9-047, and she’s not for sale.”

Dray nodded once, slow. “Noted. Still waiting.”

Miko pulled free of Brill’s grip and wiped her mouth on her sleeve. “Then we wait too.”

The lamp flickered. The shadow on the ore stretched longer, pointing straight down the grade toward the second culvert.

The shadow down the grade had knees. It limped into the lamp pool dragging a pedal-rail behind it by the seat stays, one metal wheel squealing on the ore dirt. Kass stopped six meters from the jaw, one hand braced on the rail frame, the other pressed to their bad knee. The pedal-rail was a two-seat rail bike, pedal-driven, for walking the grade when a motor died. Theirs wouldn't drive. The bearing had cooked black past the second culvert, and they'd walked the last kilometers with the chain hanging loose.

"You look like hell," Miko said.

"Thanks," Kass said. "You look like a badge someone stole and tried to polish."

Brill didn't move. "You're late."

"The rail due to fail didn't fail until after I passed it," Kass said. "Then it cooked my knee and my pride in equal measure. You still holding that door shut?"

"Trying to."

Kass reached into their coat. Not for a weapon. They pulled out Nour's tally card, stiff with grease, eleven notches cut full, C9 stamped into the steel corner. They held it out to Brill.

Brill looked at it, then at Kass's hand. She didn't take it.

"Take it," Kass said. "Eleven seals. Nour's handwriting. Culvert Nine cut in steel. That's the count you're guarding with your body."

Brill took the card. Her thumb went over the notches. "This proves nothing."

"It proves Nour struck eleven full at your jaw to pay Anza's resupply," Kass said. "It proves she confessed. It proves your storeroom is full of cans that were never yours to sell."

Brill's jaw tightened. She folded the card once, slow, and put it in her pocket. "It proves I have eleven cans and a dead reader and a man on a running board who won't cross my plate."

Kass shifted their weight off the bad knee. It didn't help. "You got two good cans out there on Dray's rail and one sweating itself to death on your pin. And now you got a tally card that says who owes who."

Dray had been still on his running board, hands folded. Now he leaned forward. The lamp light caught his face.

"Who's this?" Dray said.

"Kass," Miko said. "Node dispatcher. Pain in the ass."

"Kass," Dray said. He shifted on the rail, not standing, just turning his shoulders. "You got a name for the steel?"

Kass ignored him. They limped past Brill, past the spoiled can still dripping on the clamp pin, and stopped at the edge of Dray's pool of light. They held up the bad knee, then tapped their temple.

"I got a thread," Kass said. "You said your book was open for a name. I'm standing on the ore. Hear me out."

Dray didn't answer right away. He looked at Brill, then at the card bulging in her pocket, then back at Kass. The shadow behind Kass stretched long down the grade. The pedal-rail squeaked once, settling.

"Spell it," Dray said.
